findings.title: PodDisruptionBudget demo/web-pdb permits no disruption

evidence.note: the eviction API will reject every eviction while this is 0

findings.explanation: 1 of this budget's pods sit on the selected nodes, but the API server currently allows 0 voluntary disruptions. currentHealthy (2) equals desiredHealthy (2), so evicting any covered pod would drop the workload below its declared minimum. Every eviction will be rejected with 429 until this changes.

remediation.description: Raise the replica count so healthy pods exceed the minimum
remediation.tradeoff: costs additional capacity for the duration of the maintenance
reduces the availability guarantee the workload owner asked for; their call, not the maintenance operator's

limitations: Reflects disruptionsAllowed at the moment of the snapshot. A rollout finishing or a pod becoming ready can change it without any action here.
Covers voluntary disruption via the eviction API only. A node that fails or is deleted outright bypasses PodDisruptionBudgets entirely.

findings.title: Aggregate CPU is sufficient after removing the selected nodes

calculation.formula: free = allocatable - alreadyRequested; shortfall = needed - free

findings.explanation: The evicted pods request 50m of CPU and 1335m is free across the remaining nodes. This clears the aggregate check only — it is a necessary condition, not a guarantee that the scheduler can place every pod.
limitations: This is an aggregate sum, not a scheduling decision. Sufficient total capacity does not prove any individual pod fits on any individual node: ten nodes with 1 core free each cannot place a pod requesting 4 cores. Only the scheduler can answer that.

Scheduler predicates are not evaluated. Node selectors, affinity, taints, topology spread, and volume topology can each prevent placement regardless of free capacity. Those are covered by separate analyzers, which have their own limitations.
Uses resource *requests*, which is what the scheduler uses. A pod with no request counts as zero here and can still consume a node's actual CPU and memory at runtime.
Cordoned and not-Ready nodes are excluded from remaining capacity, since they accept no new pods.
Cluster autoscaling is not modelled. A cluster that would add nodes on demand may absorb this fine.

findings.title: Aggregate memory is sufficient after removing the selected nodes

calculation.formula: free = allocatable - alreadyRequested; shortfall = needed - free

findings.explanation: The evicted pods request 32Mi of memory and 2Gi is free across the remaining nodes. Aggregate check only.
limitations: This is an aggregate sum, not a scheduling decision. Sufficient total capacity does not prove any individual pod fits on any individual node: ten nodes with 1 core free each cannot place a pod requesting 4 cores. Only the scheduler can answer that.

Scheduler predicates are not evaluated. Node selectors, affinity, taints, topology spread, and volume topology can each prevent placement regardless of free capacity. Those are covered by separate analyzers, which have their own limitations.
Uses resource *requests*, which is what the scheduler uses. A pod with no request counts as zero here and can still consume a node's actual CPU and memory at runtime.
Memory cannot be oversubscribed the way CPU can. A pod exceeding its limit is killed, not throttled, so headroom here is less forgiving than it looks.
